nameStory: The Wood Duck earned its name from its unique habit of nesting in tree cavities, unlike most ducks that nest on the ground near water. This woodland-loving waterfowl is also called the Carolina Duck, reflecting its abundance in the southeastern United States. It's one of the few duck species that's truly at home both swimming in ponds and perching on tree branches.
description: The Wood Duck is a medium-sized duck known for being one of North America's most stunning waterfowl, especially the males. These ducks are about the size of a mallard, with a distinctive crested head and elegant profile. Males sport an incredible array of colors including iridescent greens, purples, and blues, while females are more subdued with gray-brown plumage and white markings. They're partial migrants, meaning some stay year-round while others head south for winter.

idTips.label: Male's colorful plumage
idTips.description: Breeding males are unmistakable with their iridescent green head crest, white chin strap, chestnut breast, and intricate pattern of colors that shimmer in sunlight like a living jewel

idTips.label: Distinctive head crest
idTips.description: Both males and females have a sleek, swept-back crest that gives them an elegant, almost regal appearance - like they're wearing a natural crown

idTips.label: Female's teardrop eye marking
idTips.description: Female Wood Ducks have a distinctive white teardrop-shaped patch around their dark eyes, contrasting beautifully with their warm gray-brown head

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Unlike most ducks, you'll often see Wood Ducks perched on tree branches, logs, or fence posts - their sharp claws grip surfaces that would be impossible for typical webbed-footed ducks

idTips.label: Flight profile
idTips.description: In flight, they appear compact with a square tail and broad wings, often flying through trees with surprising agility rather than just over open water

idTips.label: Squeaky call
idTips.description: Males make a distinctive rising whistle that sounds like a squeeze toy, while females give a sharp 'oo-eek' call that carries well across wooded swamps

habitat: Wood Ducks prefer wooded swamps, beaver ponds, and slow-moving streams surrounded by mature trees - especially those with natural cavities for nesting. You'll find them in forested wetlands where oak, maple, and other hardwoods provide both food (acorns and seeds) and nesting sites. They're particularly drawn to areas where water and woodland meet, from sea level up to about 2,000 feet elevation throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: April through May is prime time for spotting Wood Ducks as they return from migration and begin courtship displays. Males are in their most spectacular breeding plumage, and you might see pairs investigating tree cavities for nesting.
seasonality.summer: Look for families with adorable fuzzy ducklings following mom through quiet backwaters. Young birds jump from nest cavities high in trees within 24 hours of hatching - quite a sight if you're lucky enough to witness it.
seasonality.fall: September and October bring migrating flocks and males molting back into their brilliant colors after a dull summer eclipse plumage. Great time to see larger numbers gathering before winter.
seasonality.winter: Some Wood Ducks remain year-round in ice-free areas, though numbers are much lower. Look for them in spring-fed ponds and slow streams that don't freeze completely.

funFact: Baby Wood Ducks perform one of nature's most incredible leaps of faith - within 24 hours of hatching in tree cavities up to 60 feet high, these tiny fluffballs jump out and bounce off the ground like fuzzy ping-pong balls, completely unharmed, then toddle off to find water they've never seen before.
confusionNotes: Female Wood Ducks might be confused with female Mallards, but remember the Wood Duck's distinctive crest and white teardrop eye patch - Mallards have flatter heads and blue wing patches. Male Wood Ducks in eclipse plumage (summer molt) look similar to females but retain some iridescent coloring on their wings.
contextualKnowledge: Wood Ducks nearly went extinct in the early 1900s due to overhunting and habitat loss, but made one of conservation's greatest comeback stories thanks to hunting restrictions and nest box programs. Today, thousands of volunteers maintain nest boxes that supplement natural tree cavities, making Wood Duck conservation a true community success story.
compareHints: While Wood Ducks share the genus Aix with Mandarin Ducks (an Asian species occasionally seen as escapes in New England), Wood Ducks are the only native Aix species here. Mandarin males have different color patterns with orange 'sail' feathers, while Wood Duck males have that distinctive white chin strap and chestnut breast. Both species share the tree-nesting habit that makes them unique among North American ducks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mandarin Ducks are very closely related to our native Wood Ducks - they're the only two species in the genus Aix.
